extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalism students and practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading excerpt from a history of American journalism that articulates standards, norms, and examples of journalistic practice, ethics, editorial tactics, and the professionalization of the field. Useful as a source of criteria for evaluating journalistic conduct, editorial strategy, and professional values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the laboring or semi-educated classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The appeal to the laboring or semi-educated classes (as had been true in the thirties) produced immediate success; Evening Sun and Evening World were brought out to address not the educated class but those less fortunately conditioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tactics include large type, black headlines, afternoon/evening papers, and presentation designed to be accessible; expanding readership among previously non-reading populations can increase circulation without necessarily diminishing other papers. Example: Pulitzer's World gained hundreds of thousands in circulation by addressing this audience; conservative papers later adopted some methods to increase constituency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unprejudiced, judicial approach to reporting and editorializing
rubrics_metrics.description: "I want you to go into the Maynard case with an absolutely unprejudiced mind... I want you to get together all the documents in the case... regard yourself as a judicial officer, oath-bound to justice, and when you shall have mastered the facts and the law in the case, I want you to set them forth in a four column editorial that every reader of the World can easily understand."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master facts and law; collect all documents; study minutely as if preparing for an examination; present findings clearly and comprehensibly for general readers. Treat editorial work like judicial duty—impartial, evidence-based, and pedagogically clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concentrated editorial force to compel accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer's instruction during the 1896 bond issue: present facts clearly and conclusively, then 'compel' the Administration to heed them by concentrating editorial space and coordinating outreach until a public response forces change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics include devoting full editorial space to a single issue, setting forth facts 'in compact form and in the most effective way possible,' coordinating dispatches and public appeals, and even offering demonstrable guarantees (e.g., offering to buy bonds) to prove sincerity. The criterion emphasizes coordinated reporting+editorial advocacy to produce public-policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism as defender and upholder of democracy (public-minded mission)
rubrics_metrics.description: The model instructions are described as 'praecepta of journalism as the defender and upholder of democracy.' Journalism's mission includes holding officials to duty, exposing secret schemes of plunder, and promoting hopeful plans of progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate journalism by its civic responsibilities: serving the public weal, shaping public opinion responsibly, and acting as a watchdog. Emphasis on disinterested, public-spirited press with trained intelligence to know right and the courage to do it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sentiment and melodrama to arouse public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer 'was successful in arousing public interest' because 'what essentially appealed to him in journalism was its opportunity to touch the heart; because he was a sentimentalist he was successful in arousing public interest and establishing his papers as great, powerful, popular organs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentiment and melodramatic presentation are legitimate journalistic tools for mobilizing readers and promoting reforms (e.g., prison reform, ending petty official oppression). Critics (educated class) may label such techniques demagogy; practitioners should be aware of this trade-off and use sentiment to serve substantive public purposes rather than mere exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional training and formation of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer saw that journalists 'should be trained, as well and as thoroughly as those who entered any of the other professions' and urged the founding of a school of journalism to eliminate waste and develop character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism requires institutional education and ethical formation to prepare practitioners for responsibilities to the public. Training is not merely vocational but character-building: reduce ad-hoc career shifts and instill standards and responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devotion to simple truth; truthfulness as the primal principle
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is no profession, unless it is medicine, that calls for a higher regard for the simple truth than does journalism. 'A good reporter is one who is never deceived by a lie.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High regard for factual accuracy and skepticism toward falsehoods is central. Ethical evaluation privileges reporters who prioritize truth over fame or money. The passage frames truthfulness as an ethical imperative foundational to the profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and personal sacrifice in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Edward Marshall (wounded in front lines yet dictated his story) and Gregory T. Humes (mortally injured in a wreck but thought first of notifying his paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic valor and personal sacrifice—being present in danger to get and send news—are celebrated as professional virtues. Evaluations of reporters may account for their willingness to risk personal safety to inform the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial standards of taste and fitness for family readership
rubrics_metrics.description: James King asserted he 'would print nothing that was not fit to be read at his own fireside' and refused low medical advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standards of taste and avoid commercially tempting but ethically dubious content. Refusing certain advertisements or sensational items is part of editorial integrity; evaluate newspapers on what they deem 'fit' for general home readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted editorial tactics to expand readership and adapt methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of a large semi-educated population led to innovations (penny papers, news systems, evening papers) and tactics like larger type and black headlines to appeal to previously unserved readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial strategy by how effectively it identifies and reaches underserved audiences. Innovation/adaptation (format, typography, timing) that broadens engagement is a measurable criterion, balanced against potential loss of traditional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that partisanship/prejudice can be instrumental
rubrics_metrics.description: "Journalism is the only profession where prejudice, like versatility, may be an asset."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text acknowledges that editors like Hearst possessed 'deep ingrained prejudices' which could be strengths if the journalist's vision is correct; evaluations should consider how an editor's biases shape coverage and whether they serve or harm public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to and value of critical oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism from the educated class toward democratic journalism is natural and 'to a certain extent this is wise, because healthy, sound, vigorous criticism is as necessary for radicalism as reform is necessary for conservatism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy criticism functions as a check on journalistic excesses. Evaluate media by responsiveness to legitimate critique and by sustaining internal and external checks to preserve vigor and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/judicial standard for evaluating journalists' legacies
rubrics_metrics.description: To arrive at a correct historic judgment: conceive the man as 'thoroughly dead and completely forgotten' and ask 'Did he wield that power for good or for evil? Was he selfish? Was he... corrupt?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical figures in journalism, apply fair, evidence-based measures: examine actions and consequences rather than contemporary invective; weigh service to public interest, legality, and ethics to determine long-run judgment.
